Model studies indicate that the discharge from the proposed Bad Creek Project would travel as an interlayer wedged between the epilimnion and hypolimnion. The Bad Creek discharge would enter the lake at a depth of about 20 meters, a depth similar to the intake-discharge at the Jocassee facility (Exhibit W, Appendix J).
Applicant has proposed to construct a submerged weir about 40 to 50 feet below the water surface in the Whitewater River arm of Lake Jocassee. Model studies have shown that such a weir would help restrict withdrawal and discharge at Bad Creek to the epilimnial water of Lake Jocassee, thereby reducing the impact on coldwater habitat. Applicant states that the weir would also decrease the area of Lake Jocassee affected by the Bad Creek discharge, reduce the area needed for disposal of terrestrial excavated tunnel rock spoil, and possibily reduce entrainment of trout at Bad Creek during the warm months.
The presence of the submerged weir in the Whitewater River arm of Lake Jocassee and the operation of the proposed Bad Creek Project would be expected to retain much of the inflow from the Whitewater River in the Whitewater arm of Lake Jocassee. Therefore, this water would be unavailable as a source of cold, oxygenated water to the trout habitat in Lake Jocassee. Applicant estimates that such a loss would reduce trout habitat in Lake Jocassee by a thickness of about 0.9 reter. This estimate discounts any addition to habitat during the winter unstratified period and during the period of May through September. If it were assumed that Whitewater inflows contributed to replenishment of trout habitat in the winter period, the loss would be about 1.8 meters in thickness.
The proposed project operation would result in the weekly replacement of about 90 percent of the upper reservoir volume, with maximum water level fluctuations of 160 feet. Due to this high volume of exchange, the water in the upper reservoir should be of about the same quality as that of Lake Jocassee at the depth of withdrawal.
With the upper reservoir at maximum drawdown, its average depth would be about 62.5 feet, with a maximum depth of about 150 feet at full pool. The initial forces of the withdrawals during generation and discharges during pumping would not be sufficient to totally destroy any stratification which might exist in the deeper layers during the stratification period.
